lessons.title: Close-up: a signature and a silence

zoom.label: The stone floor at the bottom left corner

c1.text: Level one: David went back to Rome to paint it. Now zoom into the bottom left corner, on the stone floor: there's writing.

zoom.label: The stone floor at the bottom left corner

c1q.text: What place and year does David's inscription give?

sources.title: Musée du Louvre, collection record INV 3692, 'Le serment des Horaces, entre les mains de leur père' (inscription and history; our translations)
Barthélémy Jobert, 'Le Serment des Horaces (J. L. David)', Encyclopædia Universalis (our translations)
The National Gallery, London, 'Jacques-Louis David' (artist page)
E.-J. Delécluze, Louis David, son école et son temps. Souvenirs (Paris: Didier, 1855), ch. V (our translations)

c1m.text: Rome, 1784, says the canvas; the Louvre's history says finished in July 1785. Why, nobody knows.

c1a.text: Right city, but read the numerals again.

correction.tempting: The Louvre's history says he finished it in July 1785, and London's National Gallery dates it 1785.
correction.truth: The inscription reads 'L. David faciebat ROMAE anno MDCCLXXXIV': David was making it in Rome, in 1784.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: the inscription, painted lower left. Jobert (Encyclopædia Universalis) also dates the picture 1784.

c1b.text: Yes: 'L. David faciebat ROMAE anno MDCCLXXXIV', David was making it in Rome in the year 1784. MDCCLXXXIV is 1784 in Roman numerals.

c1c.text: Paris saw it in 1785, but it wasn't made there.

correction.tempting: It triumphed at the Paris Salon of 1785, where most people first heard of it.
correction.truth: David painted it in Rome, and the inscription says so: ROMAE, in Rome, with the year 1784.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: the inscription, painted lower left. National Gallery and Jobert: David went back to Rome to paint it, 1784–85.

zoom.label: The women and children on the right

c2.text: Level one: the women belong to both families. Now zoom in on them, on the right, while the men swear on the left.

zoom.label: The women and children on the right

c2q.text: What are the women doing while the men swear?

sources.title: Toledo Museum of Art, 'The Oath of the Horatii', 1786, Jacques-Louis David (its replica, 'close to the original'), description on Google Arts & Culture
E.-J. Delécluze, Louis David, son école et son temps. Souvenirs (Paris: Didier, 1855), ch. V (our translations)
Barthélémy Jobert, 'Le Serment des Horaces (J. L. David)', Encyclopædia Universalis (our translations)
Utpictura18, Aix-Marseille University, notice 013608, 'Le serment des Horaces - David' (our translations)

c2m.text: Taut men on the left, women slumped in grief on the right: two groups, two feelings.

c2a.text: Look at their eyes: none is on the swords.

correction.tempting: The raised swords are the centre of the picture, and the men all reach towards them.
correction.truth: The women look down or close their eyes, leaning together: Toledo's museum calls them 'slumped in grief and resignation'.
correction.evidence: Toledo Museum of Art, on its replica. Delécluze (1855), quoting a critic: the 'fear and anguish' of 'a mother, a beloved and children'.

c2b.text: Yes. Toledo's museum calls them 'slumped in grief and resignation'; a critic quoted by Delécluze saw 'fear and anguish'. Not one of them looks at the swords.

c2c.text: Not here: they sit apart, already grieving.

correction.tempting: With the men about to fight to the death, you'd expect wives and sisters to try to stop them.
correction.truth: They sit apart from the men, slumped and still: in Toledo's words, 'grief and resignation', not protest.
correction.evidence: Toledo Museum of Art. Jobert: the men on one side, the women and children on the other, in two separate groups.

extends.concept: Painted in Rome: the place and year David wrote on the canvas, against the Louvre's own July 1785

c1q.what_you_learn: David's inscription at lower left says he made it in Rome in 1784, while the Louvre's history has it finished in July 1785 and London dates it 1785; why he wrote 1784 is unknown.

c1q.confidence: High for the inscription (the Louvre's transcription, legible in the photo) and for Rome (four independent sources). The 1784/1785 gap is a documented conflict, stated as such; why David wrote 1784 is unknown.
c1q.notes: Ledger claims horatii-002 (inscription, Louvre record), horatii-003 (dating conflict: Louvre record and drawing record, National Gallery, Jobert), horatii-026 (Rome), horatii-030 (Salon of 1785), horatii-061 (inscription visible at lower left). The crop's label names the place only, not the answer.

c2q.confidence: High for the posture (Toledo, Delécluze's quoted critic, and the photo agree); the place 'on the right' is Utpictura18's, and plain in the photo.
c2q.notes: Ledger claims horatii-039 (Toledo, Jobert, Delécluze), horatii-006 (our looking: none looks at the swords), horatii-018 (both families, used in the level). Toledo's wording describes its replica, which it calls close to the original apart from an added distaff. The 'begging' option is a real alternative (wives and sisters of fighting men), not a sourced claim about this picture; its card states only sourced facts.
